concepts.title: Constitutional principles
concepts.meaning: Preamble ideals read with constitutional morality
bullets: The principles questions ask what the Republic formula means, and what constitutional morality adds.
The text states the ideals. Courts have used them as a check on acts that contradict the Constitution's own commitments.
Moral language here is still tied to Articles and to basic structure, not to a private code of virtue.
concepts.mains: Open with the Preamble's words, then show one judgment in which those words constrain power.
concepts.locator: Home microtheme of constitutional principles; Preamble, PDF p. 32

concepts.title: Preamble
bullets: Adopted on 26 November 1949; expresses the authority of the people.
Sets out justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, alongside the character of the Republic.
The 42nd Amendment (1976), effective 3 January 1977, added socialist, secular and integrity.
concepts.mains: Use the Preamble for aims and the date of adoption, then move to the Article that actually confers or limits the power.
concepts.locator: Preamble, PDF p. 32; footnotes on the 42nd Amendment, s. 2 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977)

concepts.title: Republic formula
bullets: Sovereign, democratic and republic formed the original description.
Socialist and secular were added by the 42nd Amendment.
Together these terms describe independence, social justice, equal civic standing across faiths, popular government and a non-hereditary head of state.
concepts.mains: Explain each term through an institution or policy: adult suffrage for democracy, social welfare for socialism, and equal citizenship for secularism.
concepts.locator: Preamble and 42nd Amendment footnote, PDF p. 32

concepts.title: Justice, liberty, equality, fraternity
concepts.meaning: What the Preamble secures, and what it does not name
bullets: Justice is social, economic and political. Economic justice is named here and worked out in Part IV, not as a Part III title.
Liberty is of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. Economic liberty is not a Preamble head.
Equality is of status and of opportunity. Fraternity assures individual dignity and, after 1977, the unity and integrity of the Nation.
concepts.mains: Organise an answer around justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, then identify the provision or institution that puts each value into practice.

concepts.title: Constitutional morality
concepts.meaning: The Constitution's own discipline, not popular sentiment
bullets: Constitutional morality draws on liberty, equality, dignity and limits on public power.
It requires reasons rooted in constitutional commitments, including when social majorities oppose a right.
For public officials, it supports lawful, accountable and impartial conduct.
concepts.mains: Define the doctrine from the Constitution and from a judgment, then apply it to a high office: what the office must refuse even if it is popular.
concepts.locator: Navtej Singh Johar, 6 September 2018, discussion of constitutional morality; Kesavananda on the identity of the Constitution

concepts.title: Navtej Johar (2018)
bullets: Section 377 of the IPC, so far as it criminalised consensual sexual acts between competent adults, was held unconstitutional.
Chandrachud J. treats constitutional morality as the reason fundamental rights place liberty and dignity beyond majoritarian government.
The case is about that penal provision and equal citizenship. It does not create a general right to same-sex marriage.
The statutory setting is the old IPC. The equality and liberty reasoning remains relevant after the penal code's replacement.
concepts.mains: Use Navtej for constitutional morality and for dignity. Do not cite it as a marriage judgment.
concepts.locator: 6 September 2018; opening holding on section 377; Chandrachud J. on constitutional morality, PDF p. 8
concepts.fullTitle: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India

concepts.title: Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
concepts.meaning: Amend, but do not destroy the basic structure
bullets: Parliament's power under Article 368 includes amendment within limits. It does not include abrogating the Constitution or destroying its identity.
The majority summary holds that the power cannot be expanded so as to repeal the Constitution or damage essential elements of its basic structure.
The Court did not insert a clause that defines basic structure as a closed list of federalism, secularism, rights and democracy.
The italicised finality words in Article 31C were struck down. That is a narrower point than the basic-structure limit itself.
concepts.mains: A Mains answer should say the power is wide and limited: addition, variation and repeal are available, and destruction of the basic structure is not.
concepts.locator: Decided 24 April 1973; majority summary, PDF p. 35; Constitution footnote to Article 31C, AIR 1973 SC 1461
concepts.fullTitle: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala

concepts.title: Minerva Mills (1980)
bullets: Decided on 31 July 1980 and reported in the 1981 Supreme Court Reports. Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment were held beyond the amending power.
New Article 368(5), claiming unlimited power to add, vary or repeal, was unconstitutional. Clause (4), shutting out judicial review of amendments, fell with it.
Section 4, which extended Article 31C from Article 39(b) and (c) to all of Part IV, was invalid. The balance of Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure.
The unamended Article 31C, confined to Article 39(b) and (c), was not the amendment the majority struck. The 2024 footnote records the section 4 invalidation.
concepts.mains: Do not read the printed words 'all or any of the principles in Part IV' as the operative shield. Minerva Mills returned the shield toward Article 39(b) and (c).
concepts.locator: 31 July 1980, reported [1981] 1 SCR; headnote and Chandrachud CJ on sections 4 and 55; Constitution footnote, AIR 1980 SC 1789
concepts.fullTitle: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India

concepts.title: Article 14
bullets: Protects every person.
Pairs equality before law with equal protection of laws.
concepts.mains: Ask whether different treatment has a defensible constitutional basis.

concepts.title: Article 19
bullets: Includes expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession.
Each freedom has its own constitutionally specified restrictions.
concepts.mains: Name the freedom and its relevant restriction clause; avoid a generic public-interest claim.

concepts.title: Article 21
bullets: Protects every person.
Deprivation must follow a legally valid procedure.
concepts.mains: Start with liberty, examine the procedure, then connect the relevant judicial interpretation.

concepts.title: Directive Principles
concepts.meaning: Part IV as the welfare-state programme
bullets: Part IV directs State policy toward welfare, justice and social transformation.
Article 37 makes the directives non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
Social-economic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups are revision aids, not constitutional subheadings.
concepts.mains: Start with the welfare objective, identify the relevant directive, assess implementation and reconcile it with rights, resources and institutional capacity.

concepts.title: Directive Principles
bullets: Article 37 distinguishes non-enforceability from their fundamental role in governance.
Article 31C concerns specified connections to Article 39(b) and (c).
concepts.mains: Examine how rights and policy goals can be pursued together.

concepts.title: Social and economic directives
concepts.meaning: Welfare, livelihoods and fair working conditions
bullets: Article 38 sets the welfare social order. Article 39 covers livelihood, material resources, concentration of wealth, equal pay, workers and children.
Article 39A adds equal justice and legal aid. Article 41 is work, education and public assistance within economic capacity.
Article 42 is humane work and maternity relief. Article 43 is the living wage, leisure and cottage industries. Article 43A is worker participation, a 42nd Amendment insertion.
concepts.mains: Connect welfare goals to the design and implementation of social protection, work and justice policies; distinguish a policy duty from an individually enforceable claim.

concepts.title: Gandhian directives
concepts.meaning: Villages, livelihoods and protection of weaker sections
bullets: Article 40 requires organisation of village panchayats as units of self-government.

Article 43's cottage-industry clause, Article 46 on Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and weaker sections, and Article 47 on nutrition, public health and prohibition sit together in the usual Gandhian reading.
Article 48 adds scientific agriculture and animal husbandry, including the cow-slaughter clause. The label is an organising aid; each duty is still its own sentence.
concepts.mains: Use village self-government, cottage industries and protection of weaker sections to discuss decentralised and inclusive development.

concepts.title: Liberal and intellectual directives
bullets: Article 44 is the uniform civil code. Article 45 is early childhood care under six, as substituted in 2002.
Article 48A is the environment. Article 49 obliges protection of monuments declared of national importance.
Article 50 separates judiciary from executive in the public services of the State. Article 51 is international peace, treaty respect and arbitration.
Article 43B, on cooperative societies, was added by the 97th Amendment and is not part of this liberal cluster.
concepts.mains: Link institutional reform, education, environment and international peace to the Constitution’s broader programme of governance.
concepts.locator: Articles 44, 45, 48A, 49, 50 and 51, PDF pp. 54–55; Article 43B by the 97th Amendment

concepts.title: Article 38
bullets: The State shall strive for a social order in which social, economic and political justice inform national life.
Clause (2), added by the 44th Amendment, adds minimising inequalities of income and eliminating inequalities of status, facilities and opportunity.
This is a directive of governance, not a court-enforceable right.
concepts.mains: Cite Article 38 when economic justice is traced from the Preamble into Part IV.
concepts.locator: Article 38, PDF p. 52; clause (2) by the 44th Amendment, s. 9

concepts.title: Article 39
concepts.meaning: Livelihood, resources, and concentration of wealth
bullets: Policy must secure an adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work, and protection of workers and children.
Clause (b) directs distribution of the material resources of the community to the common good.
Clause (c) directs that the economic system not concentrate wealth and the means of production to the common detriment.
concepts.mains: Assess whether resource distribution and economic policy advance the common good, while respecting rights and the limits explained in Article 31C case law.

concepts.title: Article 39A
concepts.meaning: Equal justice and free legal aid
bullets: The State shall shape the legal system so that justice is not denied by economic or other disability.
Free legal aid may come by legislation, schemes, or otherwise.
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment. It is a directive, not itself a Fundamental Right.
concepts.mains: Use 39A for the constitutional footing of legal aid, and keep criminal-procedure statutes on their own citations.
concepts.locator: Article 39A, PDF p. 53; inserted by the 42nd Amendment, s. 8

concepts.title: Article 43A
bullets: The State shall take steps to secure worker participation in the management of industrial undertakings.
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment, section 9, from 3 January 1977.
Equal pay and the living wage are earlier directives; they were not the 42nd Amendment addition.
concepts.mains: Use worker participation to connect economic democracy with dignity at work, alongside fair wages and safe working conditions.

concepts.title: Article 44
concepts.meaning: Effort towards a uniform civil code
bullets: The State shall endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India.
The duty is to endeavour. Article 37 keeps the directive outside direct judicial enforcement.
The Article does not itself remove personal laws or list the political conditions of a code.
concepts.mains: Frame the debate through equality, religious freedom, legal pluralism and consultation, with Article 44 supplying the constitutional objective.

concepts.title: Article 45
bullets: The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education until the age of six.
The 86th Amendment substituted this text for the older universal-education directive, effective 1 April 2010.
Ages 6 to 14 are Article 21A and the parental duty in Article 51A(k), not Article 45.
concepts.mains: Keep the three education ages apart: under six in Article 45, six to fourteen in Article 21A, and the parent's duty in Article 51A(k).

concepts.title: Article 48A
concepts.meaning: State duty on environment, forests, wildlife
bullets: The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife.
Inserted by the 42nd Amendment, section 10.
The citizen-side duty is Article 51A(g), not this Article.
concepts.mains: Pair 48A with 51A(g) and with Article 21 case law, and do not treat 48A as a self-executing ban on development.

concepts.title: Article 50
bullets: The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
It sits in Part IV, not in the Preamble or the Seventh Schedule.
It is a directive of institutional design, not a definition of the rule of law.
concepts.mains: Use judicial independence and separation from executive control to explain how institutional design protects impartial justice.

concepts.title: Article 51
bullets: The State shall endeavour to promote international peace and security and just relations between nations.
It includes respect for international law and treaty obligations, and settlement of disputes by arbitration.
The duty is in Part IV, not in the Preamble, the Fundamental Duties, or the Ninth Schedule.
concepts.mains: Connect India’s international conduct to peaceful relations, respect for international law and dispute settlement.

concepts.title: Article 31C
bullets: Operative protection concerns laws giving effect to Article 39(b) or (c).
The 2024 edition records judicial invalidation of the attempted extension to all DPSPs.
concepts.mains: Specify the directive principle and avoid claiming blanket immunity for all welfare laws.

concepts.title: Property Owners (2024)
concepts.meaning: 31C survives; not every private asset is a community resource
bullets: The majority treats Article 31C as surviving to the extent upheld in Kesavananda, after Minerva Mills invalidated the 42nd Amendment extension.
Article 39(b) can cover some privately owned resources. It does not cover every private holding.

Whether a resource is a material resource of the community depends on context, including its nature, scarcity, and the effect on well-being and concentration. The public-trust doctrine can assist that inquiry.
The reference was answered and the particular dispute was left to be dealt with on the facts. This is not a holding that private property is never reachable.
concepts.mains: Use 2024 to stop two overstatements: that Article 31C died with the 42nd Amendment, and that every private asset is already a community resource.
concepts.locator: 5 November 2024; CJI opinion paragraph 229, printed pp. 191–192; concurrence on restoring unamended Article 31C
concepts.fullTitle: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra

concepts.title: Constitutional values
concepts.meaning: Justice, liberty, equality, dignity and fraternity
bullets: The Preamble connects political institutions with social, economic and political justice.
Liberty and equality protect individual agency and equal standing.
Fraternity links personal dignity with a shared civic community; Part III and Part IV give these values concrete expression.
concepts.mains: Organise the answer by values, identify where they reinforce or constrain one another, and support each link with a relevant provision.

concepts.title: Constitutionalism
concepts.meaning: A government limited by the Constitution
bullets: A constitution, in the sense these questions use, defines and limits governmental power.
Limited government is the point, not the number of parties, federal form, or whether the head of state is nominal.
The restriction runs against the State's authority in favour of liberty. It is not a charter for restricting liberty in favour of authority.
concepts.mains: Define constitutional government as limited government, then point to one Article that does the limiting.
concepts.locator: Theme demand; Articles 13, 14, 21, 32 and 368 as the limiting devices

concepts.title: Limited government
bullets: Public power is conferred and limited by the Constitution.
Rights and legal procedures constrain arbitrary action.
Courts and representative institutions provide different forms of review and accountability.
concepts.mains: Identify the source of public power, its constitutional limits and the institution that can hold its exercise accountable.
concepts.locator: Articles 13, 14, 21 and 32; Minerva Mills on remedies

concepts.title: Article 13
bullets: Inconsistent laws are void to the extent of inconsistency.
Constitutional amendments have a distinct framework under Article 368.
concepts.mains: Identify the law and the precise right it abridges.

concepts.title: Article 32
bullets: Guarantees access to the Supreme Court to enforce Part III rights.
The Court can issue appropriate directions, orders and writs.
concepts.mains: End with the enforceable right and the remedy sought.

concepts.title: Article 368
concepts.meaning: Addition, variation or repeal, by a stated procedure
bullets: Clause (1) lets Parliament, in exercise of constituent power, amend by addition, variation or repeal, following the procedure in the Article.
A Bill may start in either House. Each House must pass it by a majority of its total membership and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting.
The President shall give assent. The clauses read do not require a prior presidential recommendation and do not create a joint sitting.
Clauses (4) and (5), which purported to bar judicial review and to deny any limit on the power, remain printed with the Minerva Mills invalidation.
concepts.mains: Separate the three modes in clause (1), the special majority, the assent duty, and the basic-structure limit that clause (5) could not abolish.
concepts.locator: Article 368(1)–(2), PDF pp. 259–260; clauses (4) and (5) and the Minerva Mills holding

concepts.title: Constitutional democracy
bullets: Popular authority is exercised through representative institutions and adult suffrage.
Participation, accountability and public reasoning help democracy function between elections.
Rights and constitutional limits protect citizens against arbitrary exercises of majority power.
concepts.mains: Assess democracy through participation, representation, accountability and protection of rights, rather than election frequency alone.

concepts.title: Article 326
concepts.meaning: Adult suffrage for the House and Assemblies
bullets: Elections to the House of the People and to State Legislative Assemblies are based on adult suffrage.
The voter must be a citizen and not less than eighteen years, subject to disqualifications on non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt or illegal practice.
This is the constitutional franchise. It is not a Fundamental Duty to vote.
concepts.mains: Use Article 326 for the democratic machinery, and do not convert a duty question into a duty to vote.

concepts.title: Adoption, 26 November 1949
bullets: The Constituent Assembly adopted, enacted and gave the Constitution on 26 November 1949.
General commencement followed on 26 January 1950, with specified provisions taking effect earlier.
concepts.mains: Distinguish constitution-making, adoption and commencement as separate stages in the transfer to a constitutional republic.

concepts.title: Commencement, 26 January 1950
bullets: Article 394 brings the remaining Constitution into force on 26 January 1950.
On that day the Preamble's operative formula was Sovereign Democratic Republic, not yet socialist or secular.
The book places the Constitution's coming into being on this date, after an Assembly formed in 1946.
concepts.mains: Status on 26 January 1950 is a Sovereign Democratic Republic. Socialist and secular arrive only with the 42nd Amendment.
concepts.locator: Article 394, PDF p. 283; textbook PDF p. 12 on 26 January 1950

concepts.title: Preamble
bullets: The Preamble is printed as the opening of the Constitution and dates its adoption.
It states aims. It does not, by itself, create an enforceable claim in the way Part III does.
Kesavananda treats the identity and basic commitments associated with it as a limit on amendment. That is not the same as enforcing the Preamble alone.
concepts.mains: Use the Preamble to frame constitutional purposes, then identify the operative provision and the limits on public power.
concepts.locator: Preamble, PDF p. 32; Kesavananda headnote on the Preamble as a possible limit on amendment

concepts.title: Commencement and repeal
concepts.meaning: Title, start, and what was repealed
bullets: Part XXII covers the short title, commencement, authoritative Hindi text and repeals.
Article 394 distinguishes provisions effective immediately from the general commencement on 26 January 1950.
Article 395 repealed the 1935 and 1947 Acts, with an express exception for the 1949 Privy Council jurisdiction statute.
concepts.mains: Explain how staged commencement supported the transition from colonial institutions to a constitutional republic.

concepts.title: Article 393
bullets: Provides the short title: Constitution of India.
Came into force immediately under Article 394.
concepts.mains: Use the title, adoption and commencement provisions together to explain the transition from colonial authority to a constitutional republic.

concepts.title: Article 394
concepts.meaning: Some Articles at once; the rest on 26 January 1950
bullets: Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393, with Article 394 itself, came into force at once.
The remaining provisions came into force on 26 January 1950, defined as the commencement.
concepts.mains: Distinguish adoption from staged commencement when explaining how the new constitutional order became operational.

concepts.title: Article 394A
bullets: The President shall publish a Hindi translation of the Constitution, signed by Constituent Assembly members, and of later English amendments.
The published translation is, for all purposes, the authoritative Hindi text.
Inserted by the 58th Amendment, effective 9 December 1987. It is not the short-title or repeal clause.
concepts.mains: Use the authoritative Hindi text to discuss access to constitutional law, while keeping constitutional translation distinct from language policy.

concepts.title: Article 395
bullets: The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, with Acts amending or supplementing the 1935 Act, are repealed.
The Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, is expressly not repealed.
Repeal is stated. A claim that no Article repeals those two Acts is incorrect.
concepts.mains: Explain constitutional continuity and change: the new Constitution replaced the colonial statutory framework through an express repeal provision.

concepts.title: Government of India Act, 1935
concepts.meaning: A federation on paper; autonomy in the provinces
bullets: Proposed an All-India Federation of provinces and princely states, with three legislative lists.
The federation and proposed central dyarchy never commenced.
Provincial autonomy replaced provincial dyarchy and operated from 1937; Congress ministries resigned in 1939, rather than provincial autonomy universally ceasing.
concepts.mains: Identify inherited administrative and federal arrangements, then contrast limited colonial accountability with popular sovereignty, rights and responsible government after 1950.
concepts.locator: Textbook PDF p. 20; repeal later recorded in Article 395

concepts.title: Constitutional amendment
concepts.meaning: A special majority, a short ratification list, and a substantive limit
bullets: Article 368 is both the power and the procedure.
Most amendments need the special majority in each House and presidential assent. A listed federal core also needs half the States.
Kesavananda and Minerva Mills add a substantive limit the text's invalidated clauses tried to deny.
concepts.mains: Separate procedure from substance. Parliament votes as a constituent body, under hurdles, and still cannot destroy the basic structure.

concepts.title: Part XX
bullets: Part XX contains Article 368, the amending power and its procedure.
It is a separate Part from Part XVIII.
Printing clauses (4) and (5) in this Part does not revive what Minerva Mills held void.
concepts.mains: Explain constitutional flexibility alongside the procedural and substantive limits that protect constitutional identity.

concepts.title: Special majority in each House
concepts.meaning: Total membership plus two-thirds present and voting
bullets: An amendment Bill may be introduced in either House.
Each House must separately approve it by a majority of its total membership and at least two-thirds of members present and voting.
The President must give assent; specified federal changes additionally require State ratification.
concepts.mains: Explain why constitutional amendment requires broader agreement than ordinary legislation; then distinguish amendments needing State ratification.

concepts.title: State ratification list
concepts.meaning: Half the States, only for listed changes
bullets: Before presidential assent, changes to Articles 54, 55, 73, 162, 241 or 279A need ratification by at least half the State Legislatures.
The same applies to Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, Chapter I of Part XI, any Seventh Schedule List, representation of States in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.
concepts.mains: Ratification is half the States, and only for the proviso list. A Union List change qualifies because it is a Seventh Schedule List; the Governor's conditions of office do not appear in that list.

concepts.title: I.R. Coelho (2007)
concepts.meaning: Ninth Schedule protection has constitutional limits
bullets: Amendments adding laws to the Ninth Schedule on or after 24 April 1973 remain open to basic-structure review.
The Court examines the effect on fundamental rights that embody the basic structure, particularly Articles 14, 19 and 21.
Insertion into the Schedule does not confer blanket immunity; the judgment also preserves specified earlier final decisions and completed transactions.
concepts.mains: Use Coelho to explain how judicial review limits attempts to insulate legislation through constitutional amendment.
concepts.fullTitle: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu

concepts.title: Article 31B
bullets: Concerns listed Acts and Regulations.
Under I. R. Coelho (2007), Ninth Schedule insertions on or after 24 April 1973 remain subject to basic-structure review.
concepts.mains: Do not assume a Ninth Schedule entry ends all constitutional scrutiny.

concepts.title: First Amendment, 18 June 1951
concepts.meaning: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule inserted
bullets: The First Amendment inserted Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule on 18 June 1951.
It sought to protect listed laws from specified Fundamental Rights challenges.
Later basic-structure case law limits that protection.
concepts.mains: Use the amendment to show the early tension between land reform, rights protection and Parliament’s amending power.

concepts.title: Ninth Schedule history
concepts.meaning: A 1951 shield, later opened to review
bullets: The Schedule was created with Article 31B by the First Amendment.
Its original point was to protect listed land-reform laws from specified rights challenges.
After Kesavananda, Coelho refuses absolute immunity for later insertions.
concepts.mains: Trace the balance between transformative land reform and rights protection from the First Amendment to basic-structure review.

concepts.title: Constitutional safeguards
concepts.meaning: Basic structure is a doctrine; judicial review is the device
bullets: The Constitution does not contain a clause that defines basic structure as federalism, secularism, fundamental rights and democracy.
Judicial review of ordinary law is built from Articles 13, 32 and 226. Review of amendments is the basic-structure doctrine.
Secularism has been called a basic feature in Bommai. That example is not a statutory definition.
concepts.mains: Distinguish review of ordinary laws under constitutional rights and competence rules from review of amendments under the basic-structure doctrine.

concepts.title: Article 226
bullets: High Courts can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other purposes.
concepts.mains: Distinguish the scope of Article 226 from Article 32.

concepts.title: S.R. Bommai (1994)
concepts.meaning: Review of President’s Rule; secularism as a basic feature
bullets: Proclamations under Article 356 are subject to judicial review.
Relevant material and constitutional purpose constrain the power; a proclamation is not an unlimited political discretion.
The judgment recognises secularism as a basic feature of the Constitution.
concepts.mains: Use Bommai to connect federal safeguards, accountable emergency powers and protection of the Constitution’s secular character.
concepts.locator: S.R. Bommai (11 March 1994), conclusions on Article 356 review and secularism
concepts.fullTitle: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India

concepts.title: Constitutional structure
concepts.meaning: Parts, Schedules and the roles they organise
bullets: Parts organise substantive provisions; Schedules supply supporting detail.
Begin with people, rights and duties, then institutions and the distribution of power.
Use the amendment and transitional provisions to understand change; omitted provisions and judicial qualifications require care.
concepts.mains: Locate the institution or power in the constitutional framework, then connect it to rights, accountability and the distribution of authority.
concepts.locator: Contents, PDF pp. 18, 27 and 28; text at Parts IXA, XVIII and XX

concepts.title: Part IX
bullets: Part IX contains the Panchayat provisions, including reservation of seats in Article 243D.
Article 243M says this Part does not, of its own force, apply to Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under Article 244.
Parliament may extend the Part to those areas by law, with exceptions, and that law is not an Article 368 amendment.
concepts.mains: Connect local self-government to participation, devolution and social inclusion; distinguish the special arrangements for Scheduled and tribal areas.

concepts.title: Part IXA
bullets: Part IXA is headed The Municipalities and begins with Article 243P.
It deals with constitution, composition, reservation, duration, powers and finances of municipalities.
Municipal powers are not left only to the Twelfth Schedule. The Part itself is the constitutional home.
concepts.mains: Connect urban self-government with devolution, representative institutions and the capacity to provide public services.
concepts.locator: Part IXA, contents and text, PDF pp. 18 and 158

concepts.title: Part XVIII
bullets: Part XVIII contains the emergency provisions, opening with Article 352.
Articles 355 and 356, on Union duty and failure of constitutional machinery, are in this Part.
Articles 358, 359 and 360 distinguish the effect on Article 19, the effect on court access, and financial emergency.
concepts.mains: Compare the trigger, parliamentary control, duration and consequences of each emergency mechanism, then assess safeguards against misuse.

concepts.title: Constitutional history
bullets: Trace the growth of central control, legislative councils and limited representation under colonial statutes.
Compare provincial dyarchy in 1919 with provincial autonomy in 1935.
Independence and the Constitution transformed the source of authority through popular sovereignty, rights and responsible government.
concepts.mains: Explain both continuity and transformation: inherited administrative arrangements were recast through popular sovereignty, Fundamental Rights and responsible government.
concepts.locator: Textbook PDF p. 20; Article 395, PDF p. 283

concepts.title: Indian Independence Act, 1947
concepts.meaning: Dominionhood, partition, and a continuing 1935 frame
bullets: The Act ended British rule from 15 August 1947 and created the Dominions of India and Pakistan.
It empowered the Constituent Assembly to frame a constitution and to repeal British statutes, including the Independence Act.
Until the new Constitution, each Dominion was governed by the 1935 Act, which the Assembly could amend. Paramountcy over princely states lapsed.
concepts.mains: Show the 1935 Act as a bridge that Article 395 later repealed, not as the Constitution that commenced in 1950.

concepts.title: Independence, 15 August 1947
concepts.meaning: Power passed; the Constitution was still ahead
bullets: British rule ended at the midnight of 14–15 August 1947.
The 1946 Constituent Assembly became the legislature of the Dominion.
The Constitution's general commencement remained 26 January 1950.
concepts.mains: Do not equate Independence Day with commencement or with the 26 November 1949 adoption.
concepts.locator: Textbook PDF p. 22; Article 394 for the later commencement

concepts.title: Article 1
concepts.meaning: India is a Union of States
bullets: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
The States and Union territories are those specified in the First Schedule, together with acquired territory.
The name and the Union formula are operative text, unlike the 1935 federation that never commenced.
concepts.mains: Use Article 1 when a history answer must show what replaced the uncommenced 1935 federation: a Union whose units are scheduled, not a compact that waited on princely accession.

concepts.title: Constitution making
bullets: Begin with the Assembly’s composition and representative limits.
Follow the Objectives Resolution, committee work and public discussion of drafts.
Distinguish adoption on 26 November 1949 from general commencement on 26 January 1950.
concepts.mains: Explain how an indirectly elected Assembly developed a democratic constitutional settlement through debate, committees, public input and negotiated agreement.
concepts.locator: Indian Polity, eighth edition, PDF pp. 26–32; Preamble; Article 394

concepts.title: Constituent Assembly of 1946
concepts.meaning: Framed the Constitution and sat as the Dominion legislature
bullets: Constituted under the Cabinet Mission scheme: provincial representatives were indirectly elected and princely-state representatives nominated.
First met on 9 December 1946, with Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary chairman; Rajendra Prasad became permanent President on 11 December.
The Drafting Committee, chaired by B.R. Ambedkar, was appointed on 29 August 1947.
After independence, the Assembly also performed the Dominion legislature’s role.
concepts.mains: Assess the Assembly through representation, deliberation and accommodation: indirect election was a limitation, while debate and consensus helped build constitutional legitimacy.
concepts.locator: Indian Polity, eighth edition, PDF pp. 26–32

concepts.title: Judicial independence and accountability
concepts.meaning: Morality binds the judge as well as the minister
bullets: Judicial independence protects adjudication from improper executive and political pressure.
Reasoned decisions, transparent procedure and fidelity to constitutional limits support accountability.
Constitutional morality requires judges and other public officials to justify power through constitutional reasons.
concepts.mains: Balance decisional independence with reason-giving, fair process and institutional accountability.
concepts.locator: Minerva Mills on limited power and judicial review; editorial Mains application

concepts.title: Fundamental Duties
concepts.meaning: All eleven clauses, without a built-in penalty
bullets: Eleven clauses organise responsibilities to the Republic, society and collective development.
The clauses apply to citizens and complement rights and Directive Principles.
Enforcement of a particular obligation or penalty depends on applicable law.
concepts.mains: Begin with the relevant clause, connect it to a civic problem, and evaluate how education, institutions and proportionate legal measures can support compliance.

concepts.title: Article 51A
bullets: Part IVA lists eleven duties of every citizen.
The 42nd Amendment added clauses (a)–(j); the 86th added the parent or guardian’s education duty in clause (k).
The duties guide civic conduct and interpretation; the Article itself provides no general penalty for non-compliance.
concepts.mains: Connect a specific duty to civic responsibility and a relevant right or directive, while distinguishing constitutional duties from penalties created by legislation.

concepts.title: Duties to the Republic
bullets: (a) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
(b) cherish the ideals of the national struggle for freedom.
(c) uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
(d) defend the country and render national service when called upon.
concepts.mains: Sovereignty, unity and integrity appear both as a duty and in the Preamble. The duty is clause (c), not a directive.

concepts.title: Duties of social conduct
bullets: (e) promote harmony and common brotherhood beyond religious, linguistic and regional diversities, and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
(f) value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
(i) safeguard public property and abjure violence.
concepts.mains: Use harmony, women’s dignity, composite culture and protection of public property to discuss responsible citizenship in a diverse society.

concepts.title: Duties of development
bullets: (g) protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and have compassion for living creatures.
(h) develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
(j) strive towards excellence in individual and collective activity.
(k) a parent or guardian must provide opportunities for education to a child or ward aged six to fourteen.
concepts.mains: Connect environment, scientific temper, excellence and education to citizens’ role in social development.

concepts.title: Article 21A
bullets: Requires free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen.
The manner of provision is determined by law.
concepts.mains: Connect the guarantee to access and implementation barriers.

concepts.title: Where a provision sits
bullets: The Constitution assigns different legal roles to guarantees, policy directives and civic duties.
Article 50 is a Directive Principle; Article 51A(f) is a citizen’s duty; Article 24 is a Fundamental Right.
Locating a provision helps identify its addressee, scope and method of enforcement.
concepts.mains: State where a provision sits, whom it binds and how it operates before assessing policy implementation.

concepts.title: Article 24
bullets: Bars employment of children below fourteen in factories, mines or other hazardous employment.
Broader statutory protection must be distinguished from this constitutional text.
concepts.mains: Link protection from exploitation to education and social support.

concepts.title: Human-rights echoes beyond Part III
bullets: Human dignity, equality and freedom connect the Universal Declaration with India’s constitutional commitments.
Part III guarantees, Part IV welfare objectives and Part IVA civic responsibilities perform distinct domestic roles.
Comparison with the Declaration does not itself establish a directly enforceable Indian constitutional claim.
concepts.mains: Compare the shared values, then distinguish international standards from the domestic guarantees and institutions through which protection is delivered.
concepts.locator: UDHR Articles 1–3, 22–29; Preamble and Parts III, IV, IVA

concepts.title: Political concepts in the Constitution
concepts.meaning: State, liberty, equality, rights, duties, separation
bullets: State, liberty, equality, rights and duties provide the vocabulary for constitutional reasoning.
Connect each idea to its legal expression and the institutions that sustain it.
Use separation of powers to examine how the Constitution distributes and controls authority.
concepts.mains: Define the concept, identify a constitutional mechanism, then show its relevance to a governance problem.
concepts.locator: Parts III and IVA; Articles 12, 14, 18, 19, 21 and 50

concepts.title: The State in political theory
bullets: Political theory identifies population, territory, government and sovereignty as elements of a State.
Government is the machinery through which the State acts; governments can change while the State continues.
Article 12 uses State in a specific constitutional sense to identify authorities bound by Part III.
concepts.mains: Define the political concept first, then distinguish it from the legal scope of State under Article 12.
concepts.locator: CBSE Legal Studies XI, Chapter 1, sections II and IV; Article 12

concepts.title: Article 12
bullets: Identifies bodies covered by “State” in Part III.
The definition includes government and local or other authorities.
concepts.mains: Identify who owes the constitutional obligation.

concepts.title: Liberty and law
concepts.meaning: Protected choice within a constitutional order
bullets: Liberty includes protected space for choice and the conditions that make meaningful choice possible.
Constitutional law both protects freedom and defines justified limitations.
Articles 19 and 21 provide concrete guarantees whose restrictions require constitutional scrutiny.
concepts.mains: Examine the freedom involved, the State’s justification and the legal safeguards that prevent a restriction from becoming arbitrary.

concepts.title: Equality as absence of privilege
concepts.meaning: A political implication, with Article 14 beside it
bullets: Equal civic standing rejects arbitrary privilege.
Article 14 combines equality before law with equal protection of laws.
Substantive equality can require attention to unequal starting points; equal treatment need not mean identical treatment in every situation.
concepts.mains: Distinguish formal equal treatment from measures addressing disadvantage, and assess whether the distinction has a justified purpose.

concepts.title: Article 18
bullets: The State cannot confer titles except military or academic distinctions.
Rules concerning foreign titles and benefits vary by citizenship and office.
concepts.mains: Distinguish prohibited titles from permitted distinctions.

concepts.title: Rights as claims against the State
concepts.meaning: Not privileges of a few, and not claims by the State
bullets: Rights are justified claims that protect interests such as liberty, dignity and equal treatment.
Many constitutional rights constrain State power; some also address conduct by private persons, as in Articles 17 and 23.
Whether a guarantee protects citizens or all persons depends on the particular provision.
concepts.mains: Identify the right-holder, the duty-bearer, the scope of the guarantee and the remedy.

concepts.title: Rights and duties travel together
bullets: Rights generate duties to respect, protect or fulfil the protected interest.
Fundamental Duties articulate citizens’ civic responsibilities.
A person does not generally lose Fundamental Rights merely because a Fundamental Duty is alleged to have been breached.
concepts.mains: Explain how rights and responsibilities reinforce one another while retaining independent constitutional safeguards.

concepts.title: Separation of powers
concepts.meaning: Distributed power with checks and balances
bullets: Distributing public power reduces the risk of arbitrary concentration.
The Indian system combines functional separation with checks, balances and areas of institutional overlap.
Article 50 directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in the State’s public services.
concepts.mains: Discuss both independence and accountability: which institution acts, what limits apply, and who can review its action?
concepts.locator: Article 50; Minerva Mills on the balance of the three wings

concepts.title: Rule of law
concepts.meaning: Limited power, equal law, and fair procedure
bullets: Public power must have legal authority and remain subject to legal limits.
Equal protection, fair procedure and accessible remedies help prevent arbitrariness.
Maneka Gandhi connects Article 21’s procedure with fairness and the guarantees of Articles 14 and 19.
concepts.mains: Assess a State action through authority, equality, fair procedure and effective review.
concepts.locator: Articles 14 and 21; Maneka Gandhi node as already sourced in the rights graph

concepts.title: Maneka Gandhi (1978)
bullets: Article 21 procedure must be fair, just and reasonable.
Read Articles 14, 19 and 21 together where applicable.
concepts.mains: Use Maneka Gandhi (1978) to connect procedural fairness with liberty and equality.
concepts.fullTitle: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
concepts.locator: Puttaswamy (2017), Chandrachud J., para 23, PDF pp. 22–23: discussion of Maneka Gandhi
concepts.status: Historical holding; supported here by later Supreme Court discussion.

concepts.title: D.K. Basu (1996)
concepts.meaning: Custody safeguards until a statute occupies the field
bullets: Custodial torture and death infringe Article 21 and the rule of law.
The Court issued requirements to be followed in arrest and detention until legislation occupied the field, starting with visible identification of the arresting police.
The requirements are judicial directions under Articles 21, 22 and 32. They are not one of the five named writs, and they are not a code of preventive-detention counsel.
concepts.mains: Use Basu for arrest procedure and Article 21. Do not use it to answer a writ-identification question.
concepts.locator: 18 December 1996; requirements beginning at PDF p. 27
concepts.fullTitle: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal

concepts.title: Constitutional remedies
concepts.meaning: Five writs and two constitutional jurisdictions
bullets: Article 32 is a fundamental right to move the Supreme Court for Part III.
Article 226 lets a High Court issue the same family of writs for rights and for other purposes.
Naming the writ is not enough. Prohibition, mandamus and quo warranto have different targets.
concepts.mains: Identify the violated right, appropriate court and remedy, then assess whether enforcement is accessible and effective.

concepts.title: Writ of prohibition
concepts.meaning: Stops a lower court exceeding its authority
bullets: Restrains a lower court or tribunal from continuing proceedings outside its jurisdiction.
Articles 32 and 226 provide the constitutional writ powers, with different scopes.
concepts.mains: Choose the remedy according to the defect and stage: prevention of an excess of jurisdiction differs from quashing an order already made.
concepts.locator: Articles 32 and 226; Indian Polity, eighth edition, PDF pp. 147–148

concepts.title: Writ of mandamus
concepts.meaning: Compels performance of a public duty
bullets: Directs performance of a public duty unlawfully left unperformed.
Under Article 226, the public character of the duty matters; private ownership alone does not settle maintainability.
Purely private contractual disputes are not converted into public-law duties merely because an organisation serves the public.
concepts.mains: Identify the public duty, the claimant’s legal entitlement and the nature of the body before deciding whether mandamus is appropriate.
concepts.locator: Ramakrishna Mission v Kago Kunya (2019), paras 21–35, discussing Andi Mukta; Articles 32 and 226

concepts.title: Writ of quo warranto
concepts.meaning: Tests the legal title to a public office
bullets: Tests the legal authority by which a person occupies a substantive public office.
Focuses on legality of appointment or eligibility, rather than policy disagreement.
A public-minded applicant need not claim the office personally; the challenge must meet the legal conditions for the remedy.
concepts.mains: Use quo warranto to connect lawful public appointments with institutional accountability.
concepts.locator: Articles 32 and 226; Indian Polity, eighth edition, PDF p. 148

concepts.title: Article 22
bullets: Ordinary arrest protections include information, counsel and production before a magistrate.
Preventive detention follows a separate constitutional framework.
concepts.mains: Distinguish ordinary arrest safeguards from preventive-detention rules.

concepts.title: Constitutional Remedies
bullets: Enforcement of Fundamental Rights through the Supreme Court.
Read the individual Articles for their holders, scope and limits.
concepts.mains: Close the analysis with an appropriate constitutional remedy.

concepts.title: Article 13 and judicial review
concepts.meaning: Law is widely defined; amendments are a separate track
bullets: Article 13 makes pre-constitutional and new law void to the extent they collide with Part III.
The definition of law is deliberately wide.
A constitutional amendment is not pulled back into Article 13 by that width. It meets the basic-structure test instead.
concepts.mains: Identify the legal instrument, the affected right and the extent of inconsistency; distinguish this inquiry from basic-structure review of amendments.

concepts.title: Inclusive meaning of law
bullets: In Article 13, law includes any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of India.
The inclusion is why an executive instrument, and not only a statute, can be tested against Part III.
Article 368(3) says Article 13 does not apply to a constitutional amendment made under Article 368. That carve-out is not a licence to destroy the basic structure.
concepts.mains: Show why constitutional review reaches subordinate legislation and legally operative customs as well as Acts of legislatures.
concepts.locator: Article 13(3)(a), PDF p. 37; Article 368(3), PDF p. 260

concepts.title: Security and rights
concepts.meaning: Article 355 is a duty, not a rights waiver
bullets: Article 355 states the Union’s protective duty toward States.
Security measures still require lawful authority and applicable constitutional safeguards.
Preventive detention has distinct Article 22 rules, while judicial scrutiny and Article 21 remain important safeguards.
concepts.mains: Balance the security objective with legal authority, necessity, procedural safeguards and meaningful review.

concepts.title: Article 355
concepts.meaning: Union duty to protect every State
bullets: The Union shall protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance.
It shall also ensure that the government of every State is carried on according to the Constitution.
The Article creates a duty. It does not create a proclamation and it does not suspend Part III.
concepts.mains: Call it a duty of protection and constitutional continuity. Do not call it an emergency by another name.

concepts.title: Article 356
concepts.meaning: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
bullets: Addresses inability to carry on a State government according to the Constitution, on a Governor’s report or otherwise.
Permits specified executive and legislative changes but does not transfer High Court powers to the President.
Normally requires approval of both Houses within two months and six-month renewals, generally up to three years.
Continuation beyond one year requires the Article 356(5) emergency and Election Commission conditions; the text retains a historical Punjab exception.
concepts.mains: Use constitutional breakdown, parliamentary checks and judicial review to assess whether an exceptional intervention is justified.

concepts.title: Article 22(3) to (4)
concepts.meaning: Preventive detention is a separate track
bullets: Clauses (1) and (2), on grounds, counsel of one's choice, and production before a magistrate within 24 hours, do not apply to an enemy alien or to preventive detention.
That exclusion is not a statement that the State need never arrange legal aid, and it is not a suspension of Article 21.
The operative clause (4) still speaks of three months and an Advisory Board. The two-month text in the 44th Amendment is printed as not yet brought into force.
concepts.mains: Balance preventive security needs against procedural safeguards, communication of grounds, representation and judicial scrutiny.
concepts.locator: Article 22(3)–(4), PDF pp. 42–43, including the unnotified 44th Amendment substitution

concepts.title: Emergency provisions
bullets: Article 352 is the national emergency. Article 356 is failure of State machinery. Article 360 is financial emergency.
Article 358 affects Article 19 automatically, and only in a war or external-aggression emergency.
Article 359 requires a presidential order and cannot touch Articles 20 and 21.
concepts.mains: Compare each emergency’s trigger, approval, duration and effects, then use constitutional and judicial safeguards to assess potential misuse.

concepts.title: Article 352
bullets: Triggered by war, external aggression or armed rebellion, including imminent danger, for all or part of India.
Requires the Union Cabinet’s written decision.
Normally needs approval of both Houses within one month, then renewal every six months, by the prescribed special majority.
Lok Sabha disapproval requires revocation; special rules address its dissolution.
concepts.mains: Compare the security trigger with written advice, parliamentary control, time limits and protection against abuse.

concepts.title: Article 357
bullets: Where Article 356 has moved legislative power to Parliament, Parliament may confer the State law-making power on the President and allow delegation.
Laws may confer duties on the Union.
If the House of the People is not in session, the President may authorise State expenditure from the Consolidated Fund pending parliamentary sanction.
concepts.mains: Article 357 is the machinery behind the statement that Parliament, or the President under its authority, legislates for the State.

concepts.title: Article 358
concepts.meaning: Article 19 yields only in a war or external-aggression emergency
bullets: Applies during a national emergency declared on grounds of war or external aggression, not armed rebellion.
The Article 19 protection it relaxes is limited to qualifying emergency-related laws and executive action under those laws.
The law must contain the required recital linking it to the emergency; ordinary unrelated action is not automatically immunised.
When the emergency ends, the temporary protection ends, subject to the saving for things already done.
concepts.mains: Distinguish the ground, affected right, required emergency connection and duration of protection; compare this mechanism with Article 359.

concepts.title: Article 359
bullets: A Presidential order can suspend access to courts for specified rights during an emergency.
Articles 20 and 21 are excluded from this power.
concepts.mains: Distinguish the right from the ability to move a court to enforce it.

concepts.title: Article 360
bullets: Addresses a threat to financial stability or credit of India or a part of it.
Normally requires approval of both Houses within two months, with special rules for Lok Sabha dissolution.
Once approved, it continues until revoked without the six-month renewal rule of a national emergency.
Authorises financial directions, including specified salary reductions and reservation of certain State financial bills.
concepts.mains: Distinguish financial emergency from national emergency and President’s Rule by its trigger, controls and consequences.

concepts.title: Right to property now
concepts.meaning: Article 300A, after the omission of Article 31
bullets: Article 31 was omitted by the 44th Amendment. The current guarantee is Article 300A.
Any person, not only a citizen, is protected, and only against deprivation without authority of law.
Article 31C still matters for laws giving effect to Article 39(b) or (c). It is not a revival of property as a fundamental right.
concepts.mains: Distinguish protection against unlawful deprivation from the State’s power to regulate and distribute resources under valid law.

concepts.title: Article 300A
concepts.meaning: Property may be taken only by authority of law
bullets: No person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.
The clause is in Part XII, Chapter IV, inserted by the 44th Amendment from 20 June 1979.
It is a constitutional legal right for any person. It is not a Fundamental Right, and it is not confined to citizens.
concepts.mains: Use Article 300A to assess the legal authority for deprivation of property, and connect it to fair governance and the distribution of resources.

concepts.title: Article 31
bullets: Article 31 was omitted by the 44th Amendment.
The constitutional property guarantee is now in Article 300A, outside Part III.
concepts.mains: Do not describe property as a current Fundamental Right.

concepts.title: Scheduled Tribes
concepts.meaning: A Presidential list, State by State
bullets: Who is a Scheduled Tribe is a constitutional notification, not a Governor's recognition.
The list is territorial.
Parliament, not the State executive, changes the list.
concepts.mains: Distinguish constitutional recognition of a community from territorial administration and the policy measures attached to recognised status.

concepts.title: Article 342
bullets: For a State, the President specifies Scheduled Tribes by public notification after consultation with the Governor.
The specification is in relation to that State or Union territory. A community can be a Scheduled Tribe in one State and not in another.
Parliament may by law include or exclude. The Governor does not make the declaration.
concepts.mains: Distinguish identification of Scheduled Tribes from territorial administration and the benefits attached to recognised status.

concepts.title: Article 244
concepts.meaning: Fifth Schedule areas and Sixth Schedule areas
bullets: Clause (1) applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Clause (2) applies the Sixth Schedule to the tribal areas in those four States.
Article 244A separately allows an autonomous State in certain tribal areas of Assam. It is not the Fifth Schedule.
concepts.mains: Compare territorial protection under the Fifth Schedule with the autonomous council institutions of the Sixth Schedule.

concepts.title: Fifth Schedule
concepts.meaning: Scheduled Areas stay under the State, with special controls
bullets: Governs Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes outside the four States covered by Article 244(2).
The President declares Scheduled Areas; Governors report on their administration and Tribes Advisory Councils advise on tribal welfare.
The Governor may regulate land transfer by or among Scheduled Tribes, land allotment to them and money-lending to them.
Regulations require presidential assent; a Tribes Advisory Council, where it exists, must be consulted.
concepts.mains: Assess whether protective administration secures land, livelihoods and participation; distinguish the Governor’s regulatory power from ordinary legislation.

concepts.title: Sixth Schedule
concepts.meaning: Tribal areas of four north-eastern States
bullets: Applies to specified tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
District and Regional Councils have specified law-making powers over matters such as land, non-reserved forests, village administration, inheritance and social customs.
Paragraph 3 laws require the Governor’s assent; powers vary with specific amendments and territorial arrangements.
District Councils may manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets and other listed services under paragraph 6.
concepts.mains: Connect autonomy with protection of culture and local decision-making, then assess accountability, resources and coordination with State institutions.
concepts.locator: Article 244(2); Sixth Schedule, paragraphs 3 and 6, including territorial modifications

concepts.title: Why the Fifth and Sixth Schedules exist
concepts.meaning: Protection of Scheduled Tribes, by two different designs
bullets: Both Schedules are about administration of tribal areas and the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
They do not fix ordinary inter-State boundaries, and they are not the Panchayat Part.
They do not protect every border State as a class.
concepts.mains: Compare protective administration and territorial autonomy, then assess participation, land protection and institutional accountability.
concepts.locator: Article 244 and the two Schedule headings

concepts.title: Scheduled areas and tribal safeguards
bullets: Distinguish recognised tribal status from the territorial designation of a Scheduled or tribal area.
Compare Fifth Schedule protection with Sixth Schedule council powers.
Panchayat reservation and the special application rules in Article 243M are separate constitutional questions.
concepts.mains: Identify the community, territory and applicable institution before explaining a safeguard; avoid treating all tribal areas as one legal category.

concepts.title: Article 243D
concepts.meaning: Panchayat seats for Scheduled Castes, Tribes, and women
bullets: Reserves directly elected Panchayat seats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population; these seats may be allotted by rotation.
At least one-third of SC/ST reserved seats must be reserved for women of those groups.
At least one-third of all directly elected seats must be reserved for women, including those reserved within SC/ST seats.
Article 243M separately governs Part IX application to Scheduled and tribal areas.
concepts.mains: Connect representation with substantive participation, while checking the special application rules for Scheduled and tribal areas.
concepts.locator: Article 243D, PDF p. 152; Article 243M(1) and (4)(b), PDF p. 126

concepts.title: Scheduled Areas
concepts.meaning: Presidential order, Governor's report, State executive power
bullets: The President declares the area. The Governor reports to the President.
The State does not lose its executive power, and a local body does not take over total administration.
Land-transfer control is a power to regulate, with presidential assent. It is not an automatic nullity for every mining lease.
concepts.mains: Walk paragraph by paragraph: who notifies, who reports, whose executive power remains, and what a regulation can do.

concepts.title: Constitutional languages
concepts.meaning: Recognition, official use and linguistic safeguards
bullets: The Eighth Schedule recognises languages; it does not alone determine official use.
Different Articles address Union and State administration, courts and legislative texts.
Mother-tongue instruction and linguistic-minority safeguards connect language policy with inclusion.
concepts.mains: Distinguish recognition from official use, then balance administrative access, linguistic diversity and minority protection.

concepts.title: Eighth Schedule
concepts.meaning: Twenty-two languages, added in named amendments
bullets: The 2024 Schedule lists twenty-two languages, ending with Urdu.
The 71st Amendment, effective 31 August 1992, inserted Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali.
Maithili was inserted with Bodo, Dogri and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment, effective 7 January 2004. It is not a 71st Amendment language.
Oriya was renamed Odia by the 96th Amendment.
concepts.mains: Distinguish recognition in the Eighth Schedule from the separate rules governing official languages, courts and minority-language education.
concepts.locator: Eighth Schedule, PDF pp. 356–357, footnotes on the 71st, 92nd and 96th Amendments

concepts.title: National honours
bullets: Article 18(1) prohibits titles other than military and academic distinctions.
Balaji Raghavan distinguishes national awards from prohibited titles.
Recipients must not use the awards as prefixes or suffixes to their names.
concepts.mains: Explain how recognition of excellence can coexist with equality of civic status, subject to limits preventing awards becoming titles.

concepts.title: Balaji Raghavan (1995)
concepts.meaning: National awards are not titles under Article 18
bullets: National awards such as Bharat Ratna and the Padma awards are not titles prohibited by Article 18(1).
They must not be used as prefixes or suffixes to a recipient’s name.
The judgment distinguishes recognition of excellence from a hereditary or status-conferring title.
concepts.mains: Use the case to reconcile equality of civic status with recognition of exceptional public contribution.
concepts.fullTitle: Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India

concepts.title: Citizenship
concepts.meaning: One Union citizenship, regulated by parliamentary law
bullets: India has a single citizenship; Part II addressed citizenship at the Constitution’s commencement.
The Citizenship Act supplies continuing acquisition and loss rules under Parliament’s Article 11 power.
Dated rules and orders change administration within statutory eligibility requirements.
concepts.mains: Distinguish constitutional membership, statutory routes and administrative procedure, then examine inclusion, fairness and accountability.
concepts.locator: Articles 5, 11 and 58; Citizenship Act sections 9 and 10

concepts.title: Article 5
bullets: At the commencement, a person domiciled in India was a citizen if born in India, or if either parent was born in India, or if ordinarily resident for at least five years before commencement.
Domicile here is a commencement test. The Article does not say that India has only one domicile for all later purposes.
Articles 6 to 10 deal with migration, persons abroad, voluntary foreign citizenship, and continuance. They are the rest of the commencement code.
concepts.mains: Article 5 answers who was a citizen on day one. Later acquisition and loss are Article 11 and the Citizenship Act.

concepts.title: Article 11
bullets: Nothing in Part II derogates from Parliament's power to make law on acquisition and termination of citizenship and on all other citizenship matters.
The Citizenship Act, 1955, is the exercise of this power.
A later processing rule does not amend Article 11. It sits under the Act.
concepts.mains: When a gazette changes a form or a route, locate the power in Article 11 and the section of the Act, not in a new constitutional citizenship.

concepts.title: Article 58
concepts.meaning: The President must be a citizen, not a citizen by birth
bullets: Eligibility is citizenship of India, age of thirty-five, and qualification for the House of the People.
The Article does not say 'citizen by birth'.
Holding an office of profit is a separate bar, with the stated exceptions.
concepts.mains: Reject the claim that only a citizen by birth can be Head of State.

concepts.title: Citizenship Act, 1955
bullets: Provides routes through birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory.
Birth rules depend on date and parentage; residence or birth alone does not settle every case.
Sections 8, 9 and 10 distinguish renunciation, termination on voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship and deprivation on specified grounds.
Section 6B supplies a particular registration or naturalisation route subject to statutory eligibility.
concepts.mains: Identify the route, relevant date, eligibility and authority before assessing acquisition or loss of citizenship.
concepts.locator: Citizenship Act, 1955, sections 3–10; MHA January 2026 compilation

concepts.title: Citizenship Rules amendment, 11 March 2024
bullets: The 11 March 2024 rules established an electronic application and scrutiny framework for section 6B.
They operate under the Citizenship Act; they do not amend Article 11.
The August 2026 instruments change processing in specified territories, so this event is a dated procedural milestone.
concepts.mains: Separate substantive eligibility in legislation from the administrative procedure prescribed by rules.
concepts.locator: Gazette text, PDF p. 29, New Delhi, 11 March 2024, G.S.R. 172(E)

concepts.title: CAA processing change (2026)
concepts.meaning: A collector route for section 6B applications
bullets: From the 19 August 2026 gazettes, section 6B registration and naturalisation applicants ordinarily resident in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, West Bengal, Assam except tribal areas, Tripura except tribal areas, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh follow a Collector route.
The application is electronic. Verification, enquiry, oath and eligibility remain. Pending committee applications are transferred as the order provides.
This changes processing. It does not rewrite who is eligible, and it does not amend Article 11.
concepts.mains: Describe a change of route and a transfer of pending applications. Do not describe a new class of citizens.
concepts.locator: Citizenship Rules amendment, rule 11A(6), gazette PDF p. 3; order S.O. 4583(E), gazette PDF p. 2; both 19 August 2026

concepts.title: Access to justice
concepts.meaning: Legal aid, fair procedure and accessible reporting
bullets: Article 39A directs equal justice and legal aid; Articles 21 and 22 protect liberty and fair treatment.
BNSS section 173 allows recording cognizable information irrespective of where the offence occurred.
Access depends on usable institutions, accountable procedure and effective remedies.
concepts.mains: Identify the barrier to justice, the constitutional or statutory safeguard and the practical reform needed to make it effective.
concepts.locator: Article 39A; BNSS section 173 in the BPRD edition, p. 105

concepts.title: BNSS section 173
bullets: Information about a cognizable offence may be given to the officer in charge of a police station irrespective of where it occurred.
Oral information is written down, read over and signed; electronic information must be signed within three days to be taken on record.
Recording information and territorial responsibility for investigation are distinct procedural questions.
Non-cognizable information follows the separate procedure in section 174.
concepts.mains: Use accessible reporting of cognizable offences to discuss barriers to justice, procedural accountability and protection of victims.
concepts.locator: BNSS sections 173–174, BPRD annotated edition, printed pp. 105–106

concepts.title: Education in the Constitution
concepts.meaning: A right, a directive, a duty, and a shared subject
bullets: Article 21A guarantees education for ages six to fourteen; Article 45 addresses early childhood care below six.
Article 51A(k) places an education duty on parents or guardians.
Concurrent legislative competence, State devolution to Panchayats and Sixth Schedule council powers are distinct governance arrangements.
concepts.mains: Connect the child’s age and entitlement with the responsible government, delivery institution and the capacity needed for effective access.
concepts.locator: Articles 21A, 45 and 51A(k); List III entry 25; Eleventh Schedule items 17–19

concepts.title: Concurrent List entry 25
concepts.meaning: Education is a shared legislative subject
bullets: List III entry 25 places education in the Concurrent List, subject to the specified Union List entries.
The 42nd Amendment shifted the principal education entry from the State List.
Eleventh Schedule items 17–19 cover education, vocational training and adult education; actual Panchayat responsibilities depend on State devolution under Article 243G.
concepts.mains: Separate legislative competence, responsibility for delivery and actual devolution of functions and funds.
concepts.locator: Seventh Schedule, List III, entry 25, PDF p. 323; Eleventh Schedule items 17–19

concepts.title: Equality and reservation
bullets: Distinguish reservations in education and public employment and identify the enabling constitutional clause.
SC/ST claims and administrative efficiency must be considered within the constitutional framework.
Davinder Singh concerns SC sub-classification; Janhit Abhiyan concerns the EWS amendment.
concepts.mains: Identify the form of disadvantage, the legal route, evidence supporting the measure and safeguards for equality and effective administration.
concepts.locator: Articles 16 and 335; Davinder Singh, 1 August 2024; Janhit Abhiyan, 7 November 2022

concepts.title: Article 16
bullets: Guarantees citizens equality of opportunity in public employment.
Reservation-related clauses have distinct requirements.
concepts.mains: Keep public employment separate from educational admission.

concepts.title: Article 15
bullets: Protects citizens against specified grounds of discrimination.
Clauses permit specified special provisions, including for women and children.
concepts.mains: Distinguish prohibited discrimination from measures advancing substantive equality.

concepts.title: Article 335
concepts.meaning: SC and ST claims, consistently with efficiency
bullets: SC/ST claims in Union and State services must be considered consistently with administrative efficiency.
The proviso permits specified relaxation of qualifying marks or standards for SC/ST reservation in promotion.
Davinder Singh explains efficiency in a manner compatible with inclusion and substantive equality.
concepts.mains: Explain how the Constitution considers SC/ST claims in public services alongside administrative efficiency, including its express proviso on promotion-related relaxation.
concepts.locator: Article 335 and proviso; Davinder Singh (2024), CJI conclusions, paragraph 205

concepts.title: Davinder Singh (2024)
bullets: The Chief Justice's conclusions hold that sub-classification of Scheduled Castes is permissible if there is a rational principle with a nexus to the purpose, and data on inadequate representation.
Sub-classification must not give all the reserved seats exclusively to a favoured sub-group. It does not amend the Presidential list.
E.V. Chinnaiah, which had forbidden sub-classification, is overruled on that holding.
These conclusions do not impose an automatic creamy-layer exclusion as a binding condition of every sub-classification.
concepts.mains: State the data-and-reason test. Do not add a creamy-layer mandate the conclusions do not contain, and do not confuse this case with the EWS amendment.
concepts.locator: 1 August 2024; CJI conclusions at paragraph 205, printed pp. 138–140
concepts.fullTitle: State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh

concepts.title: Janhit Abhiyan (2022)
bullets: A 3–2 majority upheld the 103rd Amendment enabling EWS reservation under Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
The majority accepted economic criteria and the amendment’s exclusion of classes already covered by the specified reservation provisions.
It upheld the additional reservation ceiling of ten per cent in this constitutional setting; this is not a general repeal of every reservation limit.
concepts.mains: Use the majority and dissent to examine competing accounts of substantive equality, exclusion and the limits of affirmative action.
concepts.locator: Janhit Abhiyan (7 November 2022), Maheshwari J., conclusions on the three questions; majority disposition
concepts.fullTitle: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India

concepts.title: Substantive equality
bullets: Formal equal treatment and corrective measures answer different problems.
Article 15 contains specific enabling provisions.
concepts.mains: Explain how a targeted measure advances equality, then examine its design.
concepts.relationNote: Editorial application; not an independent constitutional article.

concepts.title: Gender justice
concepts.meaning: Equality provisions, kept case by case
bullets: Articles 14–16 protect equality; Article 15(3) specifically permits special provisions for women and children.
Workplace safety, equal livelihood opportunities and recognition of gender identity require different legal and institutional measures.
Judgments help connect formal guarantees with lived exclusion and dignity.
concepts.mains: Move from the specific disadvantage to the constitutional guarantee, the relevant case principle and the implementation gap.

concepts.title: Vishaka (1997)
bullets: Sexual harassment of working women was held to violate gender equality and Articles 14, 19 and 21.
The Court laid down guidelines to fill the legislative vacuum, to be treated as law until Parliament acted.
The case is historical gap-filling. It is not a claim that workplaces are still governed only by those guidelines.
concepts.mains: Use Vishaka for the constitutional basis of protection from workplace harassment, and say the guidelines were pending legislation.
concepts.locator: 13 August 1997; opening holding on Articles 14, 19 and 21

concepts.title: NALSA (2014)
concepts.meaning: Transgender persons are 'persons' under the equality code
bullets: Recognised third-gender status and the constitutional protection of transgender persons.
Upheld the right to self-identified gender as male, female or third gender.
Directed governments to address exclusion in education, public employment, health and social welfare.
concepts.mains: Connect legal recognition with dignity, autonomy and the practical measures needed to secure equal participation.
concepts.fullTitle: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India

concepts.title: Environmental jurisprudence
concepts.meaning: Rights, public duties and sustainable development
bullets: Article 48A guides State action and Article 51A(g) addresses citizens’ environmental responsibilities.
Article 21 provides a rights perspective on environmental harm.
Vellore Citizens links sustainable development with precaution and the polluter-pays principle.
concepts.mains: Combine the right, State duty and civic duty with a relevant judicial principle, then assess implementation and distributional impacts.

concepts.title: Vellore Citizens (1996)
concepts.meaning: Precaution and the polluter, inside sustainable development
bullets: The precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle were held to be part of Indian environmental law.
Precaution means anticipating and preventing harm; scientific uncertainty is not a reason to postpone measures. The polluter bears restoration costs, including the cost of harm.
Sustainable development is the frame. It is not a holding that all development is barred.
concepts.mains: Use Vellore for the two principles and for their limit. Do not invent a separate industrial-disaster holding from a case that is not in this set.
concepts.locator: 28 August 1996; headnote and PDF p. 3 on precaution and polluter pays
concepts.fullTitle: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India

concepts.title: Article 36
bullets: Uses the same meaning of State as Part III unless the context requires otherwise.
concepts.mains: Identify the constitutional authorities responsible for applying the directives before evaluating a policy failure.

concepts.title: Article 37
